tldr: Quillmesh sells safety for event-driven systems: the free `qmc` CLI catches breaking changes between producers and consumers before deploy, and the paid Cloud makes that work across dozens of teams.
The mechanism in one line: each service declares what it produces and what it consumes, CI compares every change against what consumers actually rely on, and `can-i-deploy` gates the release.
The moat is the consumer view. A schema registry checks a producer against its own history; contract testing checks it against the real readers.

Open core: the CLI is free (Apache-2.0), Cloud costs $29 per connected service per month since July 2026, Enterprise is custom. Developer adoption is the top of the revenue funnel, so developer relations is a revenue role here.
Numbers worth quoting, with their labels: 9,400 GitHub stars and 182,000 September downloads (verified), over 300 paying customers (claimed), $22M raised in total.
Fresh news: v3.0 replay mode (September 2026), per-service pricing (July 2026), and a June postmortem for a false negative that they handled in the open.
The live risk is open-core trust: an August community thread pushed back on moving the compatibility matrix to Cloud. Expect a question on it.
Traps: not Kafka-only since 2025, not called Quillcheck since 2024, not priced per seat since July 2026, and not $25M raised.
Your angle: you lived their customer's pain (the 2022 schema incident at Brindlebay) and solved it the way their product does, then you made developers fast at Zelvora (3 days to 40 minutes).
The gaps to own honestly: no direct reports yet and no open-core experience. Bring the meetup team of 4 and the friction report loop as your leadership evidence.

what_it_is: Quillmesh is a Lisbon-based developer-tools company founded in 2022. It makes `qmc`, an open-source contract-testing CLI for event-driven systems (Kafka, NATS and AMQP), and Quillmesh Cloud, a paid hosted service built on top of it. The pitch in one line: catch breaking changes between services that talk through events before they reach production, not after.
Its buyers are platform engineering teams at companies running dozens of services. Its users are the backend engineers who write the producers and consumers.
how_it_works: Each service declares what it produces and what it consumes in a contract file, `quill.yaml`, with message schemas in JSON Schema or Avro. A producer contract says: I publish `order.created` with these fields. A consumer contract says: I read `order.created` and I rely on `id`, `total` and `currency`.

In CI, `qmc verify` checks a change against the contracts on the other side. Removing a field a consumer relies on, changing a type, or narrowing an enum is flagged as breaking. `qmc can-i-deploy` then answers the release question: is this version compatible with what runs in each environment? Version 3.0 adds replay mode, which records a sample of real production events and replays them against a new consumer before it ships ([docs](https://docs.quillmesh.example/concepts/how-it-works)).

The idea to say out loud: a schema registry checks that a *producer's* change is compatible with older versions of itself. Contract testing checks it against what each *consumer* actually uses. That consumer view is the moat.
business_model: Open core. The `qmc` CLI is free and Apache-2.0 licensed. Revenue comes from Quillmesh Cloud: a hosted contract registry, a compatibility matrix across all services, deploy history and alerts. The Team plan costs $29 per connected service per month and is free up to 5 services; Enterprise adds single sign-on, audit logs and an on-premises registry at custom prices.

The funnel is bottom-up: an engineer adds `qmc` to one pipeline, the team hits the coordination problem around 5 services, and Cloud becomes the shared source of truth. That is why developer relations sits close to revenue here: CLI activation is the top of the funnel.

tips: Install `qmc` and run `qmc verify` on a toy producer and consumer before the interview. One sentence that starts with "when I broke my own contract" is worth more than any amount of reading.

items.q: What problem does contract testing solve in event-driven systems?
a: In request and response APIs a breaking change fails loudly at call time. With events the producer does not know who listens, so a removed field breaks a consumer silently, sometimes hours later. Contract testing makes the hidden dependency explicit and checks it in CI, before deploy.

items.q: Schema registry versus contract testing, in two sentences?
a: A registry enforces compatibility rules on a producer's schema against its own earlier versions. Contract testing checks a change against what each consumer actually reads, so it allows a change nobody depends on and blocks one that looks harmless but breaks a real reader.

Whether this exact version of a service is compatible with the versions running in a given environment, using the verification results stored in the registry. It turns contract testing from a report into a release gate.

items.q: What is replay mode and why does it matter?
a: Shipped in v3.0 in September 2026, it records a sample of real production events and replays them against a new consumer version in CI. Contracts catch what teams declared; replay catches what they forgot to declare, like a field that is optional in the schema but always present in practice.

items.q: How do you measure developer relations in an open-core company?
a: Tie activity to the funnel: CLI installs and first successful `qmc verify` (activation), teams with 5 or more services verified (the Cloud trigger), community-sourced Cloud signups, and contributor retention. Report a small set every month and say which ones you influence directly. Talk attendance goes in an appendix.

items.q: What makes a good quickstart for a CLI like `qmc`?
a: Time to first value under 10 minutes, a working example the user did not have to write, and an error message on the first breaking change that teaches the concept. Your Zelvora quickstart rewrite is the proof you know how: 3 days to 40 minutes.

items.q: How do you turn community feedback into product input without becoming a ticket router?
a: Aggregate and rank: a monthly friction report with counts, quotes and a proposed fix, reviewed live with product. You did exactly this at Zelvora, and 7 of the items shipped in 2025.

items.q: How do you choose which conferences to attend?
a: Go where buyers and builders overlap: platform engineering and streaming events rather than general developer festivals. Judge each event by the activations that follow, using a workshop repo or a tracked link, not by badge scans.

items.q: Why per-service pricing instead of per seat?
a: Value grows with the number of services under contract, not with the number of people who log in. Per-service pricing also removes the incentive to share one login, and it maps to the moment Cloud becomes necessary, around 5 services.

items.q: What happened with the v2.7.0 release?
a: For two days in June 2026, enum narrowing was not flagged as breaking. They shipped v2.7.1, published a postmortem with a timeline and added the case to their test corpus. For a trust product, the open postmortem was the right response, and it is a good talking point.

items.q: What was the August community controversy about?
a: A proposal to show the cross-service compatibility matrix only in Cloud. Contributors read it as moving value out of the open-source tool. The CTO committed to keeping every check in the CLI open and moving only the hosted view. It is the open-core boundary question in one thread.

items.q: Who is the buyer and who is the user?
a: The buyer is the platform engineering lead who owns release safety across teams. The user is the backend engineer writing producers and consumers. Developer relations wins the user; the user's success builds the buyer's case.

positioning: **Lead with the customer's pain, lived.** In 2022 a schema change at Brindlebay broke consumers and cost 6 hours of tracking events. You introduced schema review and a compatibility check in CI, and there were zero schema incidents in the next 12 months. That is Quillmesh's pitch, told by someone who needed it.
**Then show the developer relations result.** At Zelvora you cut median time to first webhook from 3 days to 40 minutes. Activation is the metric this role will be judged on.
**Community evidence that is yours.** 14 meetups and about 600 members at Event-Driven Porto, and a maintained testing library (`kafkette`, about 300 stars). Small but real, and in the right niche.
**Languages are an EMEA asset.** Portuguese, English and Spanish, with 4 talks given in Portuguese or Spanish. The company is in Lisbon and the role covers EMEA.
**Be exact about scale.** Your numbers are modest and true. Say them precisely and never round them up.

objections.objection: This is a lead role and you have never managed anyone.
objections.reframe: True, no direct reports. What you have led: a volunteer organizing team of 4 for five years, where nobody had to follow you, and a monthly cross-functional review with product. Ask how the role grows; if the plan is to hire two people in year one, say you want a hiring plan and a manager to learn from in the first quarter.

Your users were developers integrating an events API, and their hardest problems were the ones Quillmesh solves: unclear event contracts and breaking changes. Before that you ran a Kafka pipeline and built the CI compatibility check that `qmc` replaces.

objections.objection: Have you worked in open source with a commercial edge?
objections.reframe: Not in an open-core company, and say so. You maintain a small library and you have read the August thread closely. Your view: keep every check open, sell the coordination layer. Ask how they draw that line internally.

open.q: Pitch Quillmesh in 30 seconds to a platform engineering lead.
a: Model answer: "Your services talk through events, so a producer can break a consumer it does not know about, and you find out in production. Quillmesh makes those dependencies explicit: every service declares what it produces and consumes, and `qmc` checks each change against what real consumers rely on before deploy. The CLI is free; Cloud gives your platform team one view and a release gate across every service."
Why it works: problem, mechanism, outcome and business model in four sentences, with no adjectives.

open.q: How would you measure the success of developer relations here in the first six months?
a: Model answer: one activation metric (median time from install to first successful `qmc verify`), one conversion metric (community-sourced Cloud signups, tracked by link and by survey), and one community health metric (returning contributors per month). Agree baselines in month one, report monthly, and say which ones you can move directly.
Bring your Zelvora method as proof: instrument each onboarding step, find the stall, fix it, measure again.

open.q: Walk me through a time a breaking change hurt you.
a: Model answer: the Brindlebay story in STAR form. A field removal broke three consumers silently and cost 6 hours of tracking events; you replayed the data, built schema review and a compatibility check in CI, and there were no schema incidents in the following 12 months.
Close the loop: "That is the problem `qmc` solves properly, and why I want to help other teams avoid that night."

open.q: A contributor publicly accuses the company of moving features behind a paywall. What do you do in the first 48 hours?
a: Model answer: acknowledge quickly and in public, without promising an outcome. Collect the concrete use cases in one place, bring them to product with counts the same week, and commit to a date for an answer. Then explain the decision and the reasoning, including what stays open.
Reference the August thread: the resolution (checks stay in the CLI, only the hosted view moves) is the kind of line developer relations helps draw and then explains.

mcq.q: What does a consumer contract in `quill.yaml` describe?
o: The events a service reads and the fields it relies on
The broker topics a service is allowed to create
The retry policy for messages that fail
The expected throughput in events per second
e: A consumer contract lists the events a service reads and, crucially, the fields it actually uses. That is the information a producer never has on its own, and it is what lets `qmc` decide whether a change is safe.

Example: the billing service reads `order.created` and relies on `id`, `total` and `currency`. If the orders team removes `coupon_code`, verification passes because no consumer declared it. If they rename `currency`, it fails and names the billing service.
mcq.k: Say "what consumers actually rely on" in the interview: it is the phrase that separates contract testing from schema validation.

mcq.q: A producer removes an optional field that no consumer declares. What does `qmc verify` report?
o: Compatible, because no consumer depends on the field
Breaking, because removing any field is breaking
A warning that blocks deploy until someone approves
Nothing, because optional fields are never checked
e: The check is consumer-driven: a change is breaking only if it breaks something a consumer declared. Removing a field nobody reads is compatible, which lets teams clean up schemas without fear.

Example: a registry with a strict backward rule might reject the same removal and force the team to keep dead fields forever. The answer "optional fields are never checked" is a trap: optional fields are checked like any other field as soon as a consumer declares them.
mcq.k: This is the cleanest way to explain the moat compared with a schema registry.

o: Is this version compatible with what runs in the target environment?
Has this version passed its unit tests?
Does the team have permission to deploy today?
Is the broker cluster healthy enough for a release?
e: It reads the verification results stored in the registry and checks this version against the versions currently deployed in an environment such as staging or production. The output is a yes or no the pipeline can act on.
Example: orders v42 passed against billing v17, but production still runs billing v16. `can-i-deploy --to production` says no and names billing v16, so the team ships billing first.
mcq.k: A gate, not a report: that is why platform teams pay for it.

mcq.q: What does replay mode (v3.0) catch that contracts alone miss?
o: Dependencies nobody declared, visible only in real events
Broker overload under peak traffic
Consumers that need an automatic rollback
Event payloads sent without encryption
e: Contracts only know what teams wrote down. Replay records a sample of real production events and runs them through the new consumer version in CI, so it catches the field everyone assumed but nobody declared.
Example: a field is optional in the schema but present in every real event, and a consumer quietly depends on it. A producer change that starts omitting it passes contracts but fails replay.
mcq.k: Shipped on 15 September 2026: the freshest product fact you can bring.

mcq.q: How is the Quillmesh Cloud Team plan priced today?
o: $29 per connected service per month
$29 per seat per month
$290 a month flat for up to 20 services
Free, with paid support only
e: Since 1 July 2026 the Team plan is priced per connected service. Value grows with the number of services under contract, not with the number of people who log in.

Example: a team with 12 services pays 12 times $29, about $348 a month, whether 3 or 30 engineers use the dashboard. Old blog posts still show seat pricing, which is why "per seat" is the classic trap.
mcq.k: If you quote pricing, say "per service since July": it shows you read current sources.

mcq.q: How much has Quillmesh raised in total?
o: $22M: a $4M seed and an $18M Series A
$25M across three rounds
$18M in a single Series A
$4M seed, with a Series A only rumored
e: The company blog and the lead investor's note agree: a $4M seed in 2023 and an $18M Series A in March 2026, $22M in total.
Example of the trap: one aggregator lists $25M because it adds a grant nobody confirmed. Quoting $25M in the room signals you read a secondary source and did not check it.
mcq.k: Totals are where candidates slip. Say the two rounds, then the sum.

mcq.q: Which download figure can you quote as verified?
o: 182,000 CLI downloads in September 2026, from the package registry
Over 200,000 downloads a month, from the company blog
2.4 million lifetime downloads, from a conference slide
9,400 downloads, from the repository page
e: The registry is the primary source for downloads, and it showed 182,000 for September 2026. The blog's "over 200,000" counts mirror traffic, so it is a claim, not a measurement.
Example: "About 180,000 a month according to the registry; the blog says more because it counts mirrors" is a sentence that earns trust. The 9,400 figure confuses downloads with GitHub stars.
mcq.k: Label every number as verified or claimed. Calibration is a developer relations skill in itself.

mcq.q: Why does open core make developer relations a revenue function at Quillmesh?
o: Free CLI adoption is the top of the funnel that leads to paid Cloud
Developer relations signs Enterprise contracts directly
Cloud revenue depends on conference sponsorship income
The CLI is paid and developer relations runs the trials
e: Engineers adopt the free CLI in one pipeline. Around 5 services, coordinating contracts across teams gets painful, and Cloud becomes the shared source of truth. More activated CLI users means more teams reaching that point.
Example: a tutorial that gets 500 teams to a first successful `qmc verify` matters more to revenue than a keynote, because activated teams are the ones that later outgrow the free tier.
mcq.k: Frame your work in funnel terms: activation first, Cloud conversions second.

mcq.q: Which metric best shows that a new `qmc` quickstart worked?
o: Median time from install to first successful `qmc verify`
Page views of the quickstart
GitHub stars gained in the launch week
Social media impressions of the announcement
e: Activation measures whether developers reached value, not whether they saw the content. Time to first successful verification is the closest proxy for "it worked for me".

Example: at Zelvora you measured median time to first webhook with onboarding telemetry and moved it from 3 days to 40 minutes. The method transfers directly: instrument each step, find where people stall, fix that step.
mcq.k: Your 3 days to 40 minutes story proves you already work this way.

mcq.q: The community asks for a feature the company plans to keep in Cloud. What is the best first move?
o: Collect the use cases, take them to product with counts, report back openly
Promise the community the feature will stay free
Stay silent until product decides
Ask users to open support tickets instead
e: Developer relations carries signal both ways without making promises it cannot keep. Aggregated use cases with counts give product something to decide on, and reporting back keeps trust even when the answer is no.

Example: the August 2026 thread on the compatibility matrix. The outcome (checks stay in the CLI, only the hosted view moves to Cloud) is the kind of line developer relations helps draw and then explains.
mcq.k: Never promise on behalf of product. Commit to a process and a date for an answer.

mcq.q: Which event is the best fit for the EMEA developer relations budget?
o: A platform engineering conference with a hands-on contract testing workshop
A general web development festival with a sponsor booth
A consumer electronics trade show
A partner's sales kickoff for account managers
e: The audience that matters is backend and platform engineers running event-driven systems. A workshop produces activated users you can count; a booth produces badge scans.

Example: a 90-minute workshop where 40 people run `qmc verify` on a sample repository, with a tracked link for later Cloud signups, is measurable. The same money at a general web festival reaches mostly frontend developers who never touch an event broker.
mcq.k: Pick events where buyers and builders overlap, and measure follow-up, not attendance.

mcq.q: What makes a monthly friction report useful to product teams?
o: Ranked issues with counts, real quotes and a proposed fix
A full export of every forum post that month
Only the issues raised by paying customers
A sentiment score without examples
e: Product teams act on patterns, not anecdotes. Counts show size, quotes show pain, and a proposed fix lowers the cost of saying yes.
Example: your Zelvora report listed the top 10 issues every month, and 7 shipped as fixes in 2025. That number is the evidence that the format works.
mcq.k: Bring a one-page sample of the report format to the interview if you can.

mcq.q: They ask: "Why Quillmesh?" Which story from your resume fits best?
o: The 2022 schema incident at Brindlebay and the CI check you built
Your 9 conference talks in 2024 and 2025
Mentoring 2 junior engineers at Brindlebay
Your degree in computer science
e: The Brindlebay incident is their customer's pain, lived and solved: a removed field broke consumers, 6 hours of events were lost, and you built the compatibility check that `qmc` turns into a product.

Example answer: "I have been your user without your product. In 2022 I spent a night replaying lost tracking events, then built a homemade version of what `qmc` does. I want to help other teams skip that night."
mcq.k: Lead with this story early: it answers motivation and domain knowledge at once.

mcq.q: The interviewer says: "You have never managed people." What is the honest reframe?
o: Agree, show the volunteer team of 4, ask how the role will grow
Say that mentoring 2 engineers counts as managing a team
Move the conversation to your conference talks
Argue that management experience does not matter here
e: Honesty first: the resume shows no direct reports, so claiming otherwise fails the moment they check. Then offer the closest real evidence: five years leading a volunteer organizing team, where influence without authority is the only tool.

Example: "No direct reports yet. For five years I have led four volunteers who did not have to follow me. I would want a clear hiring plan and a manager I can learn from in the first quarter." Counting mentoring as management is a stretch interviewers catch.
mcq.k: Never inflate. A named gap with a plan beats a stretched claim.

mcq.q: Which of these numbers matches your resume exactly?
o: Median time to first webhook: from 3 days to 40 minutes
About 1,000 meetup members
Over 10,000 stars across your repositories
More than 50 talks given
e: Only the time-to-first-webhook figure matches the resume. The meetup has about 600 members, your two repositories have about 1,400 stars together, and you gave 9 talks.
Example: rounding 600 up to 1,000 sounds harmless, but if the interviewer checks the meetup page, every other number you said loses credibility too.
mcq.k: Precise, modest numbers convince more than big round ones.

mcq.q: Which closing question best shows you understand the business?
o: "What usually triggers a team to move from the free CLI to Cloud?"
"How many vacation days do you offer?"
"Is the company planning to go public?"
"Could I also work on the frontend?"
e: It targets the conversion moment that links developer relations to revenue, and the answer tells you which metric you will really be judged on.
Example follow-up: if they say "around 5 services", explain how you would measure the share of active CLI teams that cross that line each month.
mcq.k: Ask questions whose answers change how you would do the job.
